subject: dominic-fike
research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-31, first run, mode create, empty baseline, no research notes or prior evidence). Opened 24 sources (one unavailable). Read in full: Interview Magazine with Curry Barker (S01), British GQ 2022 (S02), Guardian 2023 (S03), Evening Standard 2023 (S04), NME 2020 (S05), Pigeons & Planes 2019 (S06), Blackbird Spyplane 2023 (S07), Variety 2021 (S08). Transcribed: the Apple Music/Zane Lowe Naples film (S09, 49 minutes of YouTube captions plus seven segments re-transcribed from audio with Whisper medium.en), the 2026 Pigeons & Planes video (S10, 17 minutes, Whisper small.en; no captions existed), and the full Armchair Expert episode (S11, about 80 minutes of conversation, Whisper small.en plus eight segments re-transcribed with medium.en). About 45,000 words of transcript in all; copies are in ~/.cache/9takes-research/dominic-fike/ (not the repo). Secondary checks: S12-S20, S22-S25. Evidence was gathered and catalogued before a type was chosen; Types 7, 6, 9, 4, 3, 8 and 2 were each tested against it. Outcome: status ready, profile_format standard (his public record runs from 2018 and is deep; he does not qualify as an open case). Leading read Type 7 at medium confidence; Type 6 is the strongest alternative; wing left unknown. Risks: sensitive_allegations is true (criminal record, addiction and withdrawal accounts, drug use he says began at ten, parents' addiction and incarceration, domestic violence, Hunter Schafer's infidelity account, his own account of an earlier infidelity, siblings' legal and treatment matters, a young child), so the six-role jury applies. contested_typing is false: no published typing was found to contest, and the Six alternative is argued in type_hypothesis; a reviewer may escalate.

Accuracy check (2026-10-31). How To Quit Smoking was released October 30, 2026 on Columbia (15 tracks, about 40 minutes; first announced for October 9; singles 'Wallflower' August 28, 'Small Town' September 18, 'Pangea' October 19) (S15-S17, S19). 'Babydoll' reached No. 10 on the Hot 100 dated October 24, 2026, his first top 10 (S15); Wikipedia's artist page still says No. 16. The Comedy Tragedy Parody Tour began in Australia in December 2025 after a break; the North American leg ran August 15-September 30, 2026, alongside support dates for Tame Impala (S18, S17). He confirmed a son, Rocket, on April 7, 2026 (S10). He said in December 2025 he was in a relationship (Wikipedia; not opened at source; do not print). Euphoria season 3 aired in 2026 (coverage not opened reports an April 12 premiere); whether his filmed scenes aired is unverified (C17). The backlog note's 'Europe tour Feb 2027' was not verified and must not be printed; check his site before any mention. Turns 31 on December 30, 2026; use his birth year with absolute dates rather than an age where possible.

Drafting guidance. Standard profile, Type 7 leading at medium confidence; set enneagram: 7, type: ['celebrity'] per site convention, published: false. Strong verified hooks (choose one): (a) the motel scene: on a promotional shoot in July 2023 Zane Lowe took him back to the Naples motel room his family lived in, and five minutes in he said 'this is too much, should we go to fucking beach' and went swimming (S09 32:50-33:50, observed); (b) the Forest of Avalon told three times over six years, ending with 'I wanted Alice in Wonderland... I wanted there to be some sort of danger' (S06, S07, S11); (c) the 'Transformers band-aid' over a 'gash' (S11, verify audio). The central insight: hardship told as adventure is not denial of the facts (he states them flatly) but a refusal to stay inside them; it explains the costly choices (shrooms before the audition, cocaine on house arrest when 'trapped' and 'bored', yacht money, relapses) and his own late insight that success was a band-aid. Keep 'What is Dominic Fike's personality type?' with an answer of at most 60 words, e.g. 'Most likely a Type 7, held at medium confidence: his repeated move is to leave pain for stimulation and recast it as fine. Type 6 is the serious alternative, because he names safety as a lifelong problem.' Put the Six case beside the Seven case with his own security quotes (C20, C21, C24) and the discriminator (C16, C06, C11). Show what the type does not explain: the mother's 'quiet observer' (C23), not approaching people (C22), loyalty (C24), the grief he describes alone (C37). Durable spine: the 2019-2026 pattern. Use 'Babydoll' at No. 10 and the October 30, 2026 album only as the reason people are searching, dated. Target 2,000-3,500 words.

Quotation cautions. (a) S09 is YouTube auto-captions; quote only passages re-transcribed from audio (listed in its locator) or check the audio first. 'I had a really hard time sitting still in my own skin... I had my own distractions... drinking' is ZANE LOWE, not Fike. The mother passage is attributed by context; confirm on video and call her 'his mother'. (b) S10 and S11 are Whisper machine transcripts without speaker labels; several vivid lines in S11 belong to Dax Shepard or Monica Padman ('jumping off the second floor into the pool', 'arousal setting was set way too high', 'That's the great thing about coke. It makes you optimistic', the bar-mirror story). Confirm the voice on audio for 'I had a good time in jail' (00:42:30), 'I never extend that care to myself' (00:23:50; may be Shepard), 'self-defense mechanism' (01:02:30) and 'piece of shit... self-protection' (01:18:30). (c) The Los Angeles Times interview (Mikael Wood, July 6, 2023) was not opened; cite its quotes 'as reported by TheWrap' (S13). (d) The 'Babydoll' Instagram caption is quoted from Wikipedia (S24); verify before printing. (e) The British GQ piece (S02) is a US GQ interview by Samuel Hine; 'spin into a positive' and 'yachts' are the writer's words; 'Eric Clapton–funded' is GQ's attribution of the Antigua centre. (f) Variety 2021 says he was sober during season 2 filming; he later said he was using then. Present both with dates, not as a lie. (g) The 'Whatever I do, I do too much of it' Guardian headline paraphrases him; the body quote is about drugs. (h) Interviewers misstate the arrest ('punched a cop'); his account is that he tripped or knocked down an officer he thought had drawn a gun (later: a taser). (i) Do not quote the Complex/Variety Sundance lines as Variety without opening Variety's video. (j) Keep his profanity as spoken; do not tidy disfluent machine-transcribed speech into cleaner sentences he did not say.

Sensitivity. Addiction and recovery: use his words, dated; no diagnostic labels, no speculation about current sobriety or risk; do not make the benzodiazepine withdrawal crisis or 'near-death' drug line the hook or the ending, and do not connect him to Angus Cloud's death. Childhood: drug use from age ten, parents' heroin use, his mother's incarcerations and the stepfathers' violence are his accounts; state them briefly and without causal claims that trauma made his type. Family privacy: do not name his sister, and do not detail siblings' arrests, treatment or custody matters or his father's sentence; 'his mother' and 'his younger brother' suffice beyond what he has made central (his brother at the 2016 arrest). Relationships: attribute Hunter Schafer's account of infidelity to her, give his stated reason for the split (codependency, July 2023), note no response was found, and do not speculate about lyrics; do not name the earlier partner he discussed on Armchair Expert or repeat that story beyond 'he has described cheating in an earlier relationship before his 2020 rehab' if needed at all; do not report his December 2025 relationship. Child: only his words; never name or speculate about the child's mother. The 'yacht with 15-20 women' anecdote happened while he was dating Schafer; use with care or not at all. Criminal record: battery on a police officer (pleaded guilty), house arrest, failed drug test, county jail; avoid 'assaulted' as an unattributed verb.

Follow-ups before or at the next refresh: (1) confirm whether his Euphoria season 3 scenes aired (HBO credits, a reliable recap; the Men's Journal page S21 was CAPTCHA-blocked); (2) open the 'Babydoll' Instagram caption or a report quoting it; (3) find the Los Angeles Times interview of July 6, 2023; (4) look for on-record testimony from people who knew him before 2018 (Naples collaborators, his manager Reed Bennett, Kevin Abstract's June 2025 Zach Sang interview about Geezer) and the 2020 New York Times Presents documentary; (5) check How To Quit Smoking interviews from the release week (Apple Music, podcasts) for how he describes quitting and the Tay-K closer; (6) recheck the 'Babydoll' chart run and any 2027 tour dates. A Six-versus-Seven settle signal for a refresh: in a sober, settled period (fatherhood, a hit), does he describe what steadies him as people, preparation and stability he can count on (Six), or as new projects, motion and keeping things light (Seven)?

Draft stage (2026-10-31). Wrote a standard Type 7 profile (about 3,500 words, published: false). Re-verified quoted passages against cached copies: re-transcribed seven Zane Lowe film clips (motel, security, codependency, mother, closing chapter, ride, social) and three Armchair Expert windows (01:02:36-01:03:00, 01:18:26-01:19:10, 00:50:48-00:51:20) with Whisper medium.en; checked printed quotes in GQ, the Standard, the Guardian, NME, P&P 2019, Blackbird, Variety 2021 and Interview against the cached pages. Not printed because speaker turns stay ambiguous in machine transcripts: 'self-defense mechanism', 'a little bit of that self-protection', 'I never extend that care to myself'. Corrected: 'trying to cheat a connection' is Zane Lowe's phrase, which Fike agreed with. Still unverified and kept out of the article: whether his Euphoria season 3 scenes aired (C17 removed from the draft inventory; S20/S21 retained), the 'Babydoll' Instagram caption (C36 removed; S24 retained for the re-release date), the Los Angeles Times original (TheWrap attribution kept). Printed on transcript turn context only, without listening: 'I had a good time in jail' (C65), 'These dudes start flying from California' and 'Al Capone' (C66), the mother's identification in the Lowe film (C23); an audio or video check is the next verification step. Removed from the draft inventory as unused: C17, C25, C26, C31, C32, C36 (sources retained). No inherited production_pretext blockers (new profile).

Edit stage (2026-10-31). Adjudicated 47 findings from six reviewers (all escalated contested_typing; risks.contested_typing now true; sensitive_allegations stays true). Type thesis unchanged (Type 7, medium) but argued as a narrow lead: the discriminator was rewritten (danger as wonder, light retelling, clean-slate pleasure) after reviewers showed the draft's "moves away from threat" test was phobic-Six-only and contradicted by the 2016 incident, that "Brother, got you" was a promise to a showrunner who was testing him, and that the sober-period persistence claim rested on a release date and retrospective quotes. Added the strongest Six evidence (mentor, manager arrangement, stability "always in another person", studio community, 2023 tour structure) and a Nine test. New checks: Whisper medium.en re-runs of four Lowe film windows (21:58-22:43, 24:15-24:45, 33:08-33:33, 47:18-48:08) and one Armchair window (01:01:55-01:02:50); a 2 fps frame sheet of the motel exit (33:12-33:24); cached-page re-reads of P&P 2019, the Guardian, the Standard, GQ, People/Yahoo, Variety 2021, Interview, TheWrap, Variety 2025, Stereogum and ELLE. Speaker check outcome: "It's really weird. I feel like tense." is Fike by turn context; who said "Should we leave?" and the beach line is unresolved (medium re-run renders "Should we leave? / I'm down. Let's go"; frames show Lowe rising first), so the article credits neither to him. Removed from the article: Hunter Schafer's infidelity account and the "no public response" sentence (C18, C80; it was not type evidence and its placement implied a motive; her own words say he addressed it in his songs), the unverified "Cocaine's awesome" line (C75), C86, C88, C92, C93, C27 and the old discriminator C91. Sources S22/S23 retained in the record but no longer cited.

Follow-ups for the next refresh: (1) How To Quit Smoking release-week interviews (Apple Music, podcasts; November 2026): how he describes quitting, what steadies him, and how he retells recent setbacks (settle signal C96); (2) confirm whether Elliot appears in Euphoria season 3 (HBO credits or a reliable recap; C47, C113); (3) Hot 100 dated November 14, 2026 and the 2026 year-end list for the "Babydoll" peak (C34, C48); (4) listen by ear to the Armchair Expert jail banter (00:42:30) and sobriety passage (00:10:30) to confirm speaker turns (C65, C115); (5) a video or audio speaker check of the motel exit at 33:15-33:25 if the hook is ever extended to the beach line (C41); (6) on-record testimony from people who knew him before 2018 (manager Reed Bennett, Naples collaborators).

sources.title: Dominic Fike Tells Curry Barker Why He Can't Sit Still
sources.speaker: Dominic Fike in conversation with filmmaker Curry Barker (a friend and self-described fan), Interview Magazine
sources.date: 2026-10-07 (published; conversation dated Tuesday, August 11, 2026, Sherman Oaks, during tour rehearsals)
sources.locator: Q&A, opening exchange (Courtyard Marriott, vegan, "sacrifice chickens and cows"); answer on picking songs ("I have the metrics", Reed Bennett, "White Keys" found on an old phone); answer on fans vs. art ("Back in 2019, when I got a deal, I was only thinking about what other people wanted", meditation analogy, "White Keys" written drunk); answer on money and the kid ("it's always you", "I was lazy back then"); "write a song in 10 minutes, but I was just trying to flex"; "I forgot where we were going"; pressure answer ("There's no pressure in the studio... The pressure drops away if you're doing it right"); "big ass boat"; "They know I can be finicky with dates"; acting answer ("you don't want to be in people's faces too much", Dune press run); "I've never been the type of guy to intrude on anybody's shit. That's why I do all this shit myself. That's why I'm bad at asking girls out." Edit stage, 2026-10-31: "I have the metrics. Reed [Bennett, Fike's manager] will show me what people are listening to"; "Back in 2019, when I got a deal, I was only thinking about what other people wanted." Dated in print by the conversation header (Tuesday, August 11, 2026), published October 7, 2026.
sources.excerpt: "Back in 2019, when I got a deal, I was only thinking about what other people wanted." [...] "Sometimes you get influenced by other people, but you always bring it back." [...] "I would write a song in 10 minutes, but I was just trying to flex." [...] "There's no pressure in the studio. And if you're really songwriting, you don't have the space to feel any of that. It's like running." [...] "They know I can be finicky with dates." [...] "I always believe you don't want to be in people's faces too much." [...] "I've never been the type of guy to intrude on anybody's shit. That's why I do all this shit myself. That's why I'm bad at asking girls out."
sources.context: Friendly peer conversation recorded during rehearsals for the fall 2026 tour, published three weeks before How To Quit Smoking. Barker flatters him throughout; Fike drifts between jokes (Texas age-verification, porn) and serious answers and admits losing the thread. Also says he is 'trying to be vegan', that his manager shows him streaming metrics ('As much as I hate to see it'), that he has 'more time to make music' now with a kid and money, and that he got 'lucky' on acting. The page title ('Why He Can't Sit Still') is the editors', not his words. Interview's October 30, 2026 Sound Advice column reprints pull quotes from this conversation and is not an independent source.

(He describes jail, for example, like a sabbatical: 'It really was just a year off to focus on myself.')" [...] "I was going through so much then, and I was heavily addicted to so many drugs." [...] "Whatever happened was cool." [...] "I'm trying to go crazy. I'm trying to be like Lindsay Lohan. I'm trying to be annoyed at paparazzi and shit." [...] "I'm trying to get, like, annoying famous." [...] "I want those iconic pictures from back in the day. The cool stories. The fucked-up knees from all the Ecstasy. You know? I want all of it." sources.context: Cover-style profile at the height of Euphoria season 2 (the finale aired days later), while he was recording his second album upstate and dating Hunter Schafer. The writer says the 2016 charge followed 'an attempt to defuse a situation between the police and his younger brother'. Hine reports the Antigua rehab stint as Eric Clapton-funded (the Crossroads centre); that attribution is the writer's.

sources.excerpt: "Whatever drug I would do, I'd do too much of it – to [the point of] a near-death, surreal experience. I just kind of thought that was how you did drugs – to go all the way there without dying," he says. [...] "I was using at the time, but I wasn't worried. I was more like … psyched!" [...] "Idle hands are the devil's work … the cool part about the label thing is that it helped me keep my shit together in jail." [...] "All I know is I'm pushing forward regardless of expectation." [...] "I wish I could do that … be this huge pop star and have a drink and not have a bunch of anxiety. But I fucking can't do it: I tried."
sources.context: UK tour preview two months after Sunburn, which the writer says underperformed commercially. The headline phrase 'Whatever I do, I do too much of it' is a headline paraphrase; the quoted sentence in the body is about drugs. The piece calls his custody 'prison' in one place; he served county jail time (S06, S05). Written two months after Angus Cloud's death, which the writer mentions; Fike does not comment on it in the piece.

The tattoo origin here (a MacBook logo, chosen high to distract from the forehead tattoo) conflicts with the 2019 account that the apple honors his sister (S06) and with a 2023 'eyesore' explanation (S07). claims.alternative: Type 6 explains his stated security motive, his search for steadiness in people (C116, C117, C120) and the 2026 turn toward structure (C19, C95, C119); trauma and addiction explain escape in any type (C57). Most of the material is promotional self-report.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the leave-and-reframe sequence seen in the 2023 motel scene recurs in his accounts from 2019 onward.
claims.passage: Fike has been describing versions of that sequence, in other rooms and other years, since at least 2019.
claims.inference: Bridges the hook to the evidence; supported by the 2019 Forest of Avalon telling (S06) and later accounts (S07, S11).
claims.alternative: Addiction, trauma and promotional settings also produce this sequence; see type_hypothesis.against.

claims.alternative: Narration in a produced film; Fike's own accounts of motel years (C44) are consistent.

claims.inference: Captions at 00:28:25-00:28:30: "this was Dom's idea to visit a room where he and his family had lived." He chose to go back, which complicates a pure avoidance reading.
claims.alternative: A host's narration of a produced segment; whether the idea was his alone or agreed with producers is not shown.

claims.claim: In the same film, just before the motel exchange, Fike said he is not as relaxed on stage as he looks and fears people will see through a "ruse."
claims.passage: "I'm not really that relaxed," he said. "I'm always thinking that eventually people are going to figure out this like ruse, this like fake."
claims.inference: Impostor fear in his own words; head-triad fear evidence usable by both the Seven and Six readings.
claims.alternative: Wording from YouTube auto-captions 00:32:11-00:32:27 (S09 locator lists 31:30-32:40 as re-transcribed in research). Whether this exchange was filmed inside the motel room is not established; the draft says only "just before that point in the film."

claims.claim: Observed on camera (Apple Music film released July 2023): asked whether it was weird being back in the motel room, he said it was and that he felt tense.
claims.passage: "It's really weird. I feel like tense."
claims.inference: Whisper medium.en re-run on 2026-10-31 (33:08-33:33): "Is it weird being back in this room? / It's really weird. I feel, like, tense." The answer follows Lowe's question, so the speaker is Fike by turn context. The draft printed "Should we leave? I'm done." as his; the medium re-run renders the next words as "Should we leave? / I'm down. Let's go," which may be Lowe asking and Fike agreeing, so only the verified answer is quoted.
claims.alternative: Almost anyone would find that room hard, especially on camera, and the visit was a produced segment. The exit fits the Seven reading; it cannot prove it.

claims.claim: Within seconds of saying he felt tense, both men stood and left; they went to the beach, and Lowe's voiceover says Fike swam after "that really intense five, six minutes in the motel." Who proposed leaving is not established.
claims.passage: Within seconds both men were on their feet and out the door. (Who first suggested leaving is hard to tell from the audio.) They went to the beach, and in Lowe's voiceover, Fike swims after "that really intense five, six minutes in the motel."
claims.inference: Speaker check, 2026-10-31: Whisper medium.en on 33:08-33:33 gives "Should we leave? / I'm down. Let's go. / Thank you so much. Because that was... This is too much. Should we go to fucking beach? / Yeah. / Should we get the fuck out of here? / I'd love that." with no speaker labels; a 2 fps frame sheet (33:12-33:24) shows Lowe rising first at about 33:17 and the camera then following Fike, who is talking. Neither the "should we leave" nor the beach line can be assigned to Fike, so the article credits neither. Lowe's voiceover (33:28-33:40) establishes the swim and the "five, six minutes."
claims.alternative: Lowe's voiceover claims the beach as his own remedy ("Growing up in Auckland... just go to the beach"), and the opening narration planned the ending at the water (C103). The exit may have been a joint, produced decision.

claims.claim: The film's opening narration promises the day ends at the water.
claims.passage: Lowe's opening narration promises "we end the day staring at the horizon."
claims.inference: Captions at 00:00:40-00:00:51: "we start by knocking on the front door of this wild story but we end the day staring at the horizon." The beach was part of the film's plan, so it is not evidence of Fike's reflex.
claims.alternative: None needed; this limits the hook.

claims.claim: Interpretation of the motel sequence: he walked into the hard place on purpose, named the feeling plainly, then left within minutes; the author reads the exit as coming before the feeling could settle.
claims.passage: He walks into the hard place on purpose. He says what it feels like, plainly. Then he is out the door, and a few minutes later he is in the ocean. My read, which the film cannot prove, is that he was gone before the feeling could settle.
claims.inference: Rests on C102 (his idea), C11 (stated tension) and C41 (exit and swim). The motive reading is labeled as the author's.
claims.alternative: A produced segment that was always going to end at the beach (C103); anyone might leave such a room. The exit may have been Lowe's suggestion.

claims.inference: Consistent in outline across 2019-2025 and five interviewers. This is circumstance, not motive: any type argument has to show what he does with this history, not cite the history as evidence.
claims.alternative: The details shift by telling (the father 'rode off' on his brother's scooter in GQ; 'stealing his brother's electric scooter' in the Standard). Trauma of this kind produces escape, vigilance or numbing in people of every type. Sensitive: no clinical or causal language; never use it as the hook's punchline.

claims.claim: His mother was in and out of jail and his father was largely absent.

claims.claim: Tasbeeh Herwees (Pigeons & Planes, 2019) wrote that he lists the facts of his life "with no sense of drama" and that his childhood, he says, "was otherwise full of adventure."

claims.inference: Independent journalist observation of affect (see C07).

claims.claim: In 2025 he explained the Forest of Avalon trips: every time he left the house he wanted "Alice in Wonderland" and "some sort of danger."
claims.passage: "So every time I left the house, it was like, let's get into it. I wanted Alice in Wonderland... Every time. I wanted there to be some sort of danger."
claims.inference: Whisper medium re-transcription (aeseg-alice, 00:27:50-00:29:40) confirms wording; the ellipsis marks a host interjection ("Yeah, yeah"). The next line ("our arousal setting...") is Shepard's, not Fike's.
claims.alternative: Leaving a chaotic house for the woods is ordinary adolescence. Dax Shepard reads it as a high arousal set-point produced by chaos (trauma physiology, not type). The 2025 telling is shaped by a host who shares the story.

claims.claim: The Forest of Avalon told in 2019 ("imagine that it was another place") and 2023 ("like we'd traveled through time").
claims.passage: As young teenagers, he and his friends biked to a patch of land they called the Forest of Avalon to smoke weed and, in his words to Herwees, "imagine that it was another place." In 2023 he said it was "like we'd traveled through time."
claims.inference: Same story told to different interviewers years apart (Blackbird: "as 14 year olds").
claims.alternative: Ordinary adolescence; trauma reading in C57.

claims.claim: In 2025 he called it "literally an undeveloped lot" and said his home was small and its problems "so present."
claims.passage: he described it plainly ("It was literally an undeveloped lot. It was just a lot that had not yet turned into a Ritz") and then explained why it mattered: "my home was small and the problems were so present."
claims.inference: Whisper medium re-transcription (aeseg-alice).
claims.alternative: Host-shaped conversation; Shepard shares the story.

claims.claim: He played music from childhood: a guitar by about ten and teenage freestyle sessions at a friend's guest house called the Backhouse.
claims.passage: Music came early too: a guitar by about ten, then teenage freestyle sessions in a friend's guest house called the Backhouse, per the 2019 profile.
claims.inference: Herwees (2019): "By ten years old, he said, he'd acquired a guitar and learned to play it"; the Backhouse "was the guest house of his friend Stefan's home" where "they freestyled a lot." His music predates house arrest.
claims.alternative: Self-report relayed by a profile writer; no independent account of the scene was opened.

claims.claim: In 2023 he credited the studio and a music community for getting him through his teens.
claims.passage: "the thing that got me through my teenage years was like the studio and the community that I found in music in this very small town."
claims.inference: Whisper medium.en re-run of 21:58-22:43 on 2026-10-31 matches the captions; answer to Lowe's "what were your teenage years like." He credits people and a place, which the Six case can claim (C116).
claims.alternative: Also used as the film's cold open; a musician crediting music on a music promo is unsurprising. It does not exclude Seven.

claims.claim: Dax Shepard offered a trauma explanation: people raised in chaos have their "arousal setting" set too high.
claims.passage: people like them, raised in chaos, had their "arousal setting" set "way too fucking high."
claims.inference: Attributed to Shepard by turn context in the medium re-transcription ("'Cause our arousal setting was set way too fucking high"). Presented as the alternative explanation.
claims.alternative: Shepard is a host in recovery with his own frame; it is a trauma reading, not a type reading.

claims.claim: In 2016 he was charged with battery on a police officer; by his account he knocked down an officer he thought had drawn a gun (later: a taser) while the officer chased his younger brother.
claims.passage: In 2016 Fike was charged with battery on a police officer. By his account, an officer was chasing his younger brother, Fike thought the officer had drawn a gun (in 2025 he said it was a taser), and he knocked the man down.
claims.inference: GQ dates the charge to 2016 and gives the plea and house-arrest sentence; NME gives the jail and April 2018 release. The incident itself rests on his account. In 2025 he described the act as reflex: 'Immediately my instinct, boom.'
claims.alternative: The account is his alone; no police record was opened. Interviewers' paraphrases vary ('punched a cop' in Blackbird; 'assaulting' in GQ). The protective impulse toward his brother is better evidence of loyalty (6, 8, 2) than of a Seven motive. Length of the custody varies by telling ('a year'); use 'months' or 'about a year' with attribution.

claims.claim: He described his reaction as reflex: "Immediately my instinct, boom."

claims.inference: Armchair Expert 00:38:26 (Whisper small transcript), inside his own narration of the chase.
claims.alternative: Not re-transcribed with the medium model.

claims.claim: He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to house arrest.
claims.passage: He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to house arrest

claims.claim: During house arrest his then-manager David Fernandez bought him equipment, and by Fike's 2026 account he made the tape at Fernandez's mother's house.

claims.inference: P&P 2019: "His manager at the time, David Fernandez, bought him the equipment, and he began making the tape." P&P 2026 video (03:52-04:07): "David Fernandez I made it in his mom's house I was in the little sister room." GQ's "a friend's apartment" is not repeated; the article follows Fike's own account so the body and closing agree.
claims.alternative: GQ (2022) says he moved into "a friend's apartment"; the two may describe different stretches of house arrest.

claims.claim: On house arrest he felt "trapped all day" and bored, and used cocaine because it clears the system quickly.
claims.passage: "But I'm in a room all day, and I'm trapped all day."
claims.inference: Medium re-transcription (aeseg-bored). His causal chain runs from confinement and boredom to stimulation.
claims.alternative: Addiction explains using under confinement regardless of type; boredom is a classic relapse trigger. In 2023 he told the Standard he was high on cocaine while playing the tape back ('Oh my god, this is so good').

claims.claim: He used cocaine for its short detection window, finished the tape, failed a 7 a.m. drug test and was cuffed on the spot.
claims.passage: "So I start using everything I can that has a short span in your stream," he went on. He was being drug-tested, so he picked drugs that leave the body fast, cocaine among them. "Yeah, I'm bored." He was up using the night he finished the last song on the tape. At 7 a.m. he was called in for a test, failed it, and was cuffed on the spot. "I'd never been so in disbelief."
claims.inference: aeseg-bored transcript: "that has a short span in your stream. Coke's like three days, yeah?" The plain-language gloss states the logic the transcript supports; his quoted words are unchanged.
claims.alternative: Addiction explains using under confinement regardless of type.

claims.alternative: Reported by the Guardian, not from court records.

claims.claim: He served months in Collier County Jail and was released in April 2018.
claims.passage: He was held in Collier County Jail and released in April 2018
claims.inference: NME 2020; the Guardian says a year's sentence.

claims.claim: He reframes hardship positively; in 2022 he called jail "a year off to focus on myself."
claims.passage: 2022, to GQ: "It really was just a year off to focus on myself."
claims.inference: Six instances across 2020-2025, sober and not, in five outlets: the first move with pain is to turn it into an upside. This is the most repeated behavior in the record and the core of the Seven case.
claims.alternative: He also states the bad parts plainly when pressed: jail 'sucks, dude', the first six months 'I was not doing too well... I was sad' (Guardian 2023). Much of the positivity is comic performance in promotional settings, and recovery culture encourages gratitude framing. The 2025 'it's all great' line is followed by 'As long as you can handle it'.

claims.claim: In 2023 he described jail as "a purgatory" that "sucks," and said he was "not doing too well" in the first six months.

claims.inference: Shows the bad version is available to him; balances C06.

I'm not even kidding." / "Really?" / "I had a good time in jail." Attributed to Fike by turn context, not by ear; framed in print as banter with the hosts.
claims.alternative: Comic register with two hosts; not a considered assessment. The 2023 Guardian telling (C64) gives the bad version.

claims.alternative: Accounts differ on who uploaded it (Guardian: his manager; Armchair: he did, and Reed took it down), so the draft does not say.

claims.inference: Armchair 00:45:19 (Whisper small) and 00:51:00 (medium re-transcription in the draft stage). Both inside his own narration; Shepard's preceding hypothetical is not quoted.
claims.alternative: Comic register; not checked by ear.

claims.claim: Interpretation: two of the three dated tellings of jail skip past the bad version.
claims.passage: The bad version is available to him. Two of the three tellings skip past it.
claims.inference: Counts C06, C64, C65 as printed.

claims.passage: "I really needed money for her lawyer, straight up... It was like now or never," he said.
claims.inference: Family provision as a motive for the deal (C24).

claims.passage: He signed for a reported $4 million, according to the Standard
claims.inference: The Standard: "for a reported $4 million"; P&P: "rumored to be valued at around $4 million."
claims.alternative: Reported, not confirmed.

claims.passage: "That was my relationship with money. You use it to have the best time you can. I was bouncing off the walls, man. I was really f***ing up."
claims.inference: The aim he names is the best time, the most experience, 'all the way there' — appetite for intensity rather than control or image.
claims.alternative: Addiction pharmacology and sudden wealth explain much of this without any type. The yacht anecdotes are not printed.

claims.claim: Guardian 2023: "Whatever drug I would do, I'd do too much of it... to go all the way there without dying."
claims.passage: "Whatever drug I would do, I'd do too much of it – to [the point of] a near-death, surreal experience. I just kind of thought that was how you did drugs – to go all the way there without dying."
claims.inference: Appetite for intensity in his own words.
claims.alternative: Sensitive; placed mid-article, not as hook or ending.

claims.claim: In May 2022 he told GQ he wanted to be "annoying famous" and wanted "all of it", including "the fucked-up knees."
claims.passage: "I'm not even kidding. I'm trying to get, like, annoying famous." Why? "I want those iconic pictures from back in the day. The cool stories. The fucked-up knees from all the Ecstasy. You know? I want all of it."
claims.inference: What he wants from fame is the experience and the stories, including the damage — not a curated, admired image. A Three wants the polished picture; he asks for 'the fucked-up knees'. The 2026 reversal is dated growth, not a contradiction to hide.
claims.alternative: Deadpan comedy; the GQ answer to "Why?" begins "I just think it'd be dope…" before the quoted part. A Three reading would treat it as status hunger.

claims.claim: He took mushrooms before his first Euphoria audition, laughed and made fun of the room, and did not get the part.
claims.passage: For his first audition, he told GQ, he took mushrooms: "I started peaking right when me and Barbie were reading," meaning cast member Barbie Ferreira. He broke out laughing, started "making fun of everybody in the room," and didn't get the part.
claims.inference: GQ narrates and quotes him; "He didn't get the part." Barbie identified as Euphoria cast member Barbie Ferreira (GQ context).
claims.alternative: Told as comedy.

claims.claim: In Fike's 2025 account, Levinson, knowing about his drug use, offered help, called the five-year contract "a formality" and asked for a promise; Fike answered "Brother, got you," not yet understanding the show's scale.
claims.passage: Levinson also knew about the drugs. In Fike's 2025 telling, Levinson said, "We can get someone to help you, but you have to do this," called the five-year contract "a formality," and asked for a promise: "I need to know that you're not gonna like fuck me on this." Fike's answer: "Brother, got you." He was, he said, "not understanding the stakes still of this show" until he saw the budget on set.
claims.inference: Whisper medium.en re-run of 01:01:55-01:02:50 on 2026-10-31: "He's like, okay, I know that you get fucked up obviously... We can get someone to help you, but you have to do this. You're signed a five-year contract. This is a formality, but he's like, I need to know that you're not gonna like fuck me on this. I was like, brother, got you. Like I'm not understanding the stakes still of this show... when you see that budget... like 20 semis." Context matches the Guardian (S03: "We'll get you a sober coach"). "Brother, got you" is a promise of reliability to a showrunner who was testing him; the "stakes" are the show's scale. It is no longer used as type evidence.
claims.alternative: A loyalty pledge to a benefactor offering support fits Six at least as well as Seven; it does not discriminate. The "self-defense mechanism" lines that follow have an unresolved speaker split and are not printed.

claims.claim: About a year after the failed audition, Levinson came back with a character rewritten around him.
claims.passage: About a year later Sam Levinson, the show's creator, came back with a character rewritten "with the qualities of the guy you saw show up."
claims.inference: aeseg-defense and the 01:01:55 medium re-run: "Sam had rewritten this character that I showed up to read, but he wrote it with the qualities of the guy you saw show up." Variety 2021 confirms HBO came back a year later.
claims.alternative: His own account of Levinson's intent.

claims.claim: In 2021 he told Variety that Elliot is "exactly like me."
claims.passage: "He's exactly like me," he told [Variety](https://variety.com/2021/tv/news/dominic-fike-talks-new-album-and-starring-euphoria-season-2-1234962737/) in August 2021. "It's shit I would say and shit I would do."
claims.inference: Variety (August 6, 2021): "I don't have to do much acting... He's exactly like me. It's shit I would say and shit I would do." His self-identification with the rewritten character; the article does not attribute Elliot's fictional actions to him.
claims.alternative: Promotional framing of a role written around him; actors often say this.

claims.claim: He told Variety in 2021 he was sober during Euphoria season 2; in 2023 he said he was using during that production.

claims.claim: Three journalists (2019, 2022, 2023) described a lightness in how he tells hard facts; Hine notes he acknowledges dark periods, and Godwin's line describes him refusing a redemption arc by insisting he is still an addict.
claims.passage: Three journalists, writing years apart, described the same lightness. Herwees in 2019: "no sense of drama." Samuel Hine in GQ in 2022: "there's not a single difficult topic – not his family nor incarceration nor addiction – that Fike can't spin into a positive," though Hine adds that Fike "acknowledges that things got dark during that period." Richard Godwin in the Standard in 2023: "he defies any urge to shape it into a narrative of redemption." In Godwin's piece, that refusal comes with "I'll always be a drug addict."
claims.inference: Checked against cached pages: GQ's next sentence is "But he acknowledges that things got dark during that period"; the Standard's next lines are "He's clean and sober for the moment, but he doesn't take that for granted. 'I'm like a pretty bad drug addict... I'll always be a drug addict.'" Independent writers, but all promotional interviews.
claims.alternative: All three met him on promotional rounds, the setting the article names as its main confound; Godwin's observation is about refusing a tidy upside, not reaching one.

claims.claim: Interpretation: he makes hard facts light without turning them into a lesson; the observation is limited by its promotional setting.
claims.passage: That last line matters. A redemption story is a finished product, built to be admired, and he does not build one. My reading is that he makes the hard facts light without turning them into a lesson. All three writers met him on promotional rounds, though, the setting where a light touch plays best.
claims.inference: Author's reading of C07, labeled as such. Also the article's best discriminator against Three (C125).
claims.alternative: A comic temperament in interviews, not a motive; any type can be good company on a press tour.

claims.claim: Discriminator: Seven stays in front on the kind of danger he sought (wonder, not mastery), the recurring light retelling, and his pleasure in clean slates.
claims.passage: Three things keep Seven in front. The first is the kind of danger he went looking for. A counterphobic Six goes at a threat to master it, and the fear is the point. Fike describes his childhood danger as scenery for a story: "another place," "like we'd traveled through time," "Alice in Wonderland." The second is the retelling. The same hard event, jail above all, comes back in new versions over the years, and the light versions keep returning, as late as 2025. The third is the pleasure he takes in a clean slate, from "wipe everything" to "You're a baby again."
claims.inference: Replaces the draft's "moves away from threat" discriminator (removed: contradicted by the 2016 incident and built on a phobic-Six stereotype). Rests on C54/C03 (danger as wonder), C06/C64/C65 (jail retold), C112/C114 (clean slates).
claims.alternative: All three are retellings in interviews (promotional confound); a counterphobic Six can also romanticize danger; fresh starts are standard recovery advice.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) The only family testimony points elsewhere: his mother calls him 'the most passive, quiet child... the observer', with his brother as the loud one (C23). That fits a watchful Nine, Five or Six better than the busy-child picture of Seven. (2) He names a security motive in his own words, 'a big problem with security and safety' from never having a home, says money worries 'influenced decisions', places stability 'always in another person', and his fatherhood goals are property, reputation and sobriety (C20, C19). (3) Anxiety and impostor feelings recur from 2018 to 2026 (C21). (4) Across six years he does not pursue people: 'fear of rejection', lets collaborators come to him, 'never been the type of guy to intrude', 'bad at asking girls out' (C22). (5) He has been a loyal provider and protector since 22: his mother's lawyer, a house, the brother he tripped a police officer to protect, his brother's treatment (C04, C24), and possibly a habit of 'worrying about other people' while neglecting himself (C37, attribution unconfirmed). (6) Most of the 'excess' and 'escape' evidence overlaps with addiction; escape and minimization are what addiction and childhood trauma produce in any type, and a sober host (Shepard) reads his thrill-seeking as a trauma-set arousal level (C03, C08, C15). (7) His claimed restlessness outruns his output: three albums in eight years, a 2024-2025 break, 'finicky with dates' (C10). (8) The record is mostly self-report in promotional settings by a natural comic; three journalists' observations and one filmed scene are the only non-self-report behavior evidence, and the testimony (mother, Kenny Beats, Billie Eilish, Curry Barker) is brief or praise. Edit stage additions: he seeks steadiness in people (an older mentor, C116; a manager told to overrule him, C117; stability "always in another person", C138; the studio community that got him through his teens, C105); from 2023 he chose structure (leading the tour, quitting "cigarettes, sex, drugs, alcohol", a trainer, C119); his first-tour withdrawal looks like burnout or Nine (C127); and the danger-seeking and 2016 protectiveness fit a counterphobic Six (C118).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 6 explains the parts of the record Seven handles worst. Safety is an explicit, recurring concern in his own words: 'I've always had a big problem with security and safety 'cause I've moved around so much as a kid and I never really felt like I had a home' (Zane Lowe, 2023), and the 'next check' mindset shaped decisions (C20). He held out for a large deal 'now or never' to pay his mother's lawyer and promised 'I'm not gonna let anyone down' (2019). Loyalty is his most consistent virtue: to his mother, his brother, his childhood friends (he hired one as his chef), and to one manager since 2018, whom he asks to overrule him ('Don't listen to me. I'm manipulative!') (C24; S04, S11). He reports anxiety, impostor fear ('eventually people are going to figure out this like ruse'), nerves before sessions and overthinking (C21); he fears rejection and won't approach people (C22); he wants 'an older mentor' and says he is 'codependent on human beings' (C12, S09). His suspicion of men and male authority after abusive stepfathers (S06, S04, S11), his counterphobic act of knocking down an officer he thought had drawn a gun on his brother (C04), and his defiance of Naples' 'old white dudes' with face tattoos (C33) fit a counterphobic Six. Fatherhood has turned his goals toward property, reputation and stability (C19). Edit-stage correction: 'Brother, got you' (C16) was a promise of reliability to a showrunner who knew about his drug use, offered help and called the contract a formality; it fits Six at least as well as Seven and is no longer used against Six. The 'tiles' image (C10) has other people laying the floor, which Six can also claim. His security talk is tied to concrete deprivation and described as fading ('I feel safer now'). Other types tested and set aside: Nine (the quiet-observer childhood, non-intrusion, 'I'm chilling', numbing) fails on his appetite for intensity, 'I want all of it', 'all the way there without dying' and 'ride this... until the wheels fall off' (C08, C09); Four (confessional songs, impostor feeling, feeling like an 'eyesore', writing alone) fails on his refusal to dwell: he calls emotional song talk 'trying to cheat a connection', closes chapters, and found crying on command 'fucked up... horrible' (C11, C13, C14, S02); Three (wanted to 'blow up', watches metrics, 'just keeps winning') fails on his volunteered failures and his wish for messy rather than polished fame (C09, C27); Eight (excess, defiance, protecting his brother) fails on his aversion to confrontation and dominance and his deference to managers (C22; S04, S06); Two (providing for family, 'cater to other people') fails because helping is not how he describes his worth or identity, and he resists being cared for only half-jokingly (S11). The strongest Six-specific lines are in the same 2023 film as the Seven material: the wish for an older mentor (C116), stability "always in another person" (C138), and the studio community that got him through his teens (C105); plus the manager arrangement (C117) and the 2023 tour structure (C119). On "what steadies him", the dated answers lean Six.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: The kind of danger he seeks and the way he retells hardship. A counterphobic Six goes at a threat to master it, and the fear stays the point; a phobic Six seeks steadiness in trusted people and structure. A Seven seeks experience and options and recasts the pain as fine. Fike describes his childhood danger as wonder and escape ("imagine that it was another place", "like we'd traveled through time", "I wanted Alice in Wonderland... some sort of danger", C54, C03), not as confronting a threat. The same hard event comes back lighter in new versions across years and outlets (jail as "a year off" 2022, "a purgatory" 2023, "a good time" 2025, C06, C64, C65; five relapses as "all good", C73), and he takes pleasure in clean slates outside crisis ("wipe everything... Everyone knows you", 2018; "no one knows you... You're a baby again", 2025, C112, C114, C132). His appetite for intensity outside drug use ("ride this... until the wheels fall off... or else I feel like I didn't do it right", 2023, C120) sets Nine aside. Limit: this is a narrow lead. Most of the Seven evidence is retelling in promotional interviews. On what steadies him, his dated answers lean Six (C105, C116, C117, C138, C19), and the 2026 material runs toward restraint and security (C95, C28, C19). The draft's claim that the escape move persists unchanged into sober periods was withdrawn: the motel film's filming date and his sobriety then are not established (only that he described trying to be sober in the same film), and the 2025-2026 escape quotes were mostly retrospective (C13). The 2016 protective charge fits a counterphobic Six (C118). Settle signal: how he retells the next public setback a year later (C96).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: His mother's memory of a passive, quiet, watchful child (C23); his durable reluctance to approach people, from 'fear of rejection' in 2020 to 'bad at asking girls out' in 2026 (C22); a deep, steady loyalty and provider role since age 22 that a Seven reading treats as secondary (C24); a self-deprecation ('I already know I'm a piece of shit', Armchair Expert 2025; medium re-transcription leaves unclear whether 'self-protection' was his word or Shepard's, so it is not printed) that reads as shame more than lightness; grief he describes when alone ('want to literally just scream or cry', C37) that the interviews rarely show; face-tattoo origin stories that change by telling (C33); and whether the 2026 restraint (less partying, less public exposure, fatherhood, recording what he called 'the most like professional studio album I've ever done') is a Seven's growth toward focus or a sign the security motive was primary all along. A Seven with a strong Six wing would cover some of this (codependency, anxiety, loyalty), but that is a speculative refinement, not evidence; leave the wing unknown in print. Also: his first-tour withdrawal into his room (C127), and the wish for a mentor and a stable partner in the same breath as "ride this... until the wheels fall off" (C120, C138).
